newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis deepens as foreign minister quits.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis deepens as foreign minister quits.

text.p: Peru's political crisis deepened on Wednesday with the resignation of Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and President Alberto Fujimori's popularity falling to its lowest level in seven years in office.

Tudela's departure from the cabinet -- apparently due to his concern over a string of embarrassing scandals facing Fujimori -- deprived the government of one of its most respected and popular figures.
Fujimori's drop to a 23 percent approval rating showed the depth of public outrage over a phone-tapping scandal and the annulment of an Israeli-born businessman's citizenship.
Fujimori thanked Tudela for his services and named as his replacement lawyer Eduardo Ferrero Costa, a member of the team negotiating a border dispute with Ecuador.

Foreign Ministry sources said Tudela, a 41-year-old independent politician at the centre of the hostage crisis at the Japanese embassy this year, was increasingly concerned by the government's authoritarian style. His phone was one of 197 allegedly tapped by the secret service.
"He had to sacrifice much of his image during the last weeks in really compromising situations ... Trying to justify the unjustifiable is very costly," said political analyst Fernando Tuesta.
Local radio station Radio Programas del Peru said Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza had also resigned, but government spokesmen said they could not deny or confirm that version.

Tudela, who served as foreign minister since July 1995, was one of the 72 hostages held for four months by Marxist Tupac Amaru guerrillas in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima. He narrowly escaped alive after being hit by two bullets in the arm and leg and grenade shards in the shoulder when troops stormed the house on April 22.

Earlier on Wednesday, leading local pollster Apoyo said Fujimori's popularity falling 11 points in nine days to 23 percent. A poll of around 400 Lima area residents also showed that 53 percent believed the military really controled power in Peru. Only 38 percent said Fujimori held the reins.
But Fujimori dismissed as "mere speculation" accusations that he was a puppet of the military.

"I am the president of the republic, and I exercise as never before my civil mandate ... I think in these seven years it has been clear the president is the supreme head of the armed forces," he told the local America Television station.

Peru's security forces are widely accused of being behind a phone-tapping scandal revealed by the Frecuencia Latina T.V. channel, and ordering Sunday's revocation of Peruvian citizenship for the station's owner, Baruch Ivcher.

Frecuencia Latina T.V. had broken a string of stories alleging human rights abuses and corruption in the security forces, culminating in Sunday's report on phone-tapping by the secret services just one hour before a government decree stripped Ivcher of his citizenship.

The phone-tapping scandal and the cancelling of Ivcher's nationality on the grounds of bureaucratic "irregularities," sparked a wave of media and public condemnation and has become a rallying point for Peru's rejuvenated opposition.

Fujimori said the phone-tapping -- including taped conversations of himself and security adviser Vladimiro Montesinos in 1992 -- had been carried out by private parties unconnected to his intelligence services.
He blamed his current political problems on an opposition campaign to present him as a dictator running a police state.

In the Apoyo poll, Montesinos, considered Fujimori's right- hand man and his link to the military, received the approval of nine percent of respondents and the disapproval of 79 percent. Armed forces chief Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza won 15 percent approval and 67 percent disapproval. The survey gave no margin of error.
